props.title: Above Suspicion
props.initialSlug: FBI agent & bride hunt Nazi spies in wartime NYC

sections.content: Above Suspicion (1943) marks Joan Crawford's final film under her MGM contract, delivering a taut spy thriller that captures the mounting tensions of WWII-era Europe. The film, based on Helen MacInnes' 1941 novel, follows newlyweds turned amateur spies in a dangerous mission across Nazi Germany. Director Richard Thorpe, who previously directed Night Must Fall (1937), crafts a sophisticated blend of romance and espionage that stands alongside other wartime thrillers like Foreign Correspondent (1940) and Journey Into Fear (1943).

sections.content: The film represents a crucial transition in spy thriller conventions, bridging the gap between the lighter adventure-romance spy films of the 1930s like The Lady Vanishes (1938) and the grittier post-war espionage films that would follow. Crawford and MacMurray's characters navigate through a believably menacing Nazi Germany, with Conrad Veidt delivering a memorably sinister performance that echoes his work in Casablanca (1942).

The production design by Cedric Gibbons and cinematography by Robert Planck create a convincing pre-war European atmosphere, despite being filmed entirely in Hollywood during wartime restrictions. This approach influenced later studio-bound wartime thrillers like The Conspirators (1944) and Berlin Express (1948). SUBHEAD: Wartime Propaganda and Entertainment

sections.content: Like many American films produced during WWII, Above Suspicion walks a careful line between entertainment and propaganda. The film's portrayal of Nazi Germany, while melodramatic by today's standards, was considered quite bold for its time, following in the footsteps of Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939) and All Through the Night (1942).
